messages.subject: printing custom legends
parts:
Hi All

This is my first attempt at modifying the legend but somehow it is not working for me.

Code without legend  works fine
t <- ggplot(ref_gene_len, aes(x=ref_len)) + geom_density()

With manual scale color change
 t <- ggplot(ref_gene_len, aes(x=ref_len)) + geom_density(colour="below") + scale_colour_manual( "Check"  , c("below"="red"))


gives error
Error in grid.Call.graphics("L_polygon", x$x, x$y, index) : 
  invalid color name 'below'


-Abhi

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: printing custom legends
parts:
Hi:

There are three primary arguments to scale_manual(): breaks, values
and labels, but they act in concert rather than individually, which
can lead to some frustration. To keep things simple, let's suppose the
color variable is a factor. Then the breaks = argument corresponds to
the levels of the factor, the values = argument to the vector of
aesthetic values to be associated with the breaks (in this case,
colors), and the labels = argument represents the vector of text
labels that are to appear in the legend corresponding to the breaks.
The problem in your example is that you're trying to create a color
variable on the fly rather than predefining one in an aes() paragraph,
and this is rather tricky, but doable. There is an example in Hadley's
ggplot2 book to show how to do it, but you haven't followed its
prescriptions. I'll reproduce it below.

On Mon, Oct 24, 2011 at 4:56 PM, Abhishek Pratap <abhish...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi All
> This is my first attempt at modifying the legend but somehow it is not
> working for me.
> Code without legend  works fine
> t <- ggplot(ref_gene_len, aes(x=ref_len)) + geom_density()
> With manual scale color change
>  t <- ggplot(ref_gene_len, aes(x=ref_len)) + geom_density(colour="below") +
> scale_colour_manual( "Check"  , c("below"="red"))

Problem 1: colour = 'below' is not wrapped within an aes() paragraph,
so it is set to a single value in geom_density(). Unfortunately, there
is no color value labeled 'below' among the various color palettes, so
that alone triggers the error.

Problem 2 (more subtle, but important): There is a distinction in
ggplot2 between plot aesthetics that are *set* to a single value and
those that are *mapped* to a set of values. Variable plot aesthetics
are mapped and thus need to be included in an aes() call. Those that
are set are stated outside an aes() call. If your purpose was simply
to change the color of the density plot outline to red, all you need
is
ggplot(ref_gene_len, aes(x=ref_len)) + geom_density(colour="red")


Here are a couple of examples to illustrate this distinction using the
mtcars data from ggplot2.

library('ggplot2')
str(mtcars)

# Plot mpg vs. weight, colored by number of cylinders
# Note that wt, mpg and cyl are defined inside aes() because
# they can assume different values for different observations
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = cyl)) + geom_point()

# By default, cyl is numeric, so the legend uses a continuous
# color gradient. Let's set cyl to be factor instead:
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) + geom_point()

# OK, that's the starting point. Now set the colors to be red, blue and green
# using scale_colour_manual():
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) + geom_point() +
scale_colour_manual("Cylinders", breaks = levels(factor(mtcars$cyl)),
values = c('red', 'green', 'blue'))

# Notice that the colors in values = are associated to the levels of cyl
# in breaks = . The default title is also changed by the first argument to
# scale_colour_manual().
# Now, let's change the plotting character to be a filled triangle and
# increase the point size to 3 (default = 2). These aesthetics are *set*
# to a constant value outside an aes() statement but inside the call to
# the pertinent geom.

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = mpg, colour = factor(cyl))) +
geom_point(shape = 17, size = 3) +
scale_colour_manual("Cylinders", breaks = levels(factor(mtcars$cyl)),
values = c('red', 'green', 'blue'))


To show how to build up a factor incrementally, let's look at an
example from Hadley's book using the LakeHuron data.

# Generate a data frame with year labels
huron <- data.frame(year = 1875:1972, level = LakeHuron)
str(huron)

'data.frame': 98 obs. of 2 variables:
$ year : int 1875 1876 1877 1878 1879 1880 1881 1882 1883 1884 ...
$ level: Time-Series from 1875 to 1972: 580 582 581 581 580 ...

# We'll manufacture a factor variable by generating two graphs:
# level + 5 and level - 5 and assign each to a different factor level so
# that we can use scale_manual() to change its color.
# Note that the y aesthetic is not set in the ggplot() call because it
# will not be the same in every geom...but year will be.

# Don't run this part yet...
ggplot(huron, aes(x = year)) +
geom_line(aes(y = level + 5, colour = 'above')) +
geom_line(aes(y = level - 5, colour = 'below'))

# We have now created two lines with different colors for
# each line, but 'above' and 'below' are not valid color values,
# so we need to use scale_manual() to map colors to these
# generated factor levels:

# Run this:
ggplot(huron, aes(x = year)) +
geom_line(aes(y = level + 5, colour = 'above')) +
geom_line(aes(y = level - 5, colour = 'below')) +
scale_colour_manual('Direction', breaks = c('above', 'below'),
values = c('red', 'blue'))

Notice that the values assigned to breaks become the default labels in
the legend. These could be changed with the labels = argument.

I hope this helps you to better understand some of the distinctions
necessary in ggplot2.

Dennis
